html.q: What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?
html.answer: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe their meaning, like header, nav, main, article, section and footer, instead of generic divs. It helps screen readers and other assistive technology understand the page, improves SEO because search engines understand the structure, and makes code easier to read and maintain.

points.point: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe the meaning of content, such as header, nav and article.
Semantic HTML improves accessibility for screen readers.
Semantic HTML improves SEO.

html.q: What is the difference between block and inline elements?
html.answer: Block elements like div, p and h1 start on a new line and take the full available width, and you can set width and height on them. Inline elements like span, a and strong flow within text, only take the width of their content, and ignore width, height and vertical margins. inline-block flows inline but respects width and height.

points.point: Block elements start on a new line and take the full width.
Inline elements flow within text and only take up the width of their content.
Width and height do not apply to inline elements.
inline-block flows inline but accepts width and height.

html.q: How do you make a web form accessible?
html.answer: Every input needs a label associated with it through the for attribute or by wrapping it. Use the correct input types, group related fields with fieldset and legend, make everything reachable and usable by keyboard, show errors in text (not just colour) and link them with aria-describedby, and use ARIA attributes only when native HTML can't express something.

points.point: Each input should have an associated label element.
The form should be fully usable with a keyboard.
Error messages should be shown as text and linked to the field.
ARIA attributes help when native HTML is not enough.

html.q: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies?
html.answer: localStorage persists until cleared and is shared across tabs of the same origin; sessionStorage lasts only for one tab's session. Both hold around 5 MB and are only accessible from JavaScript. Cookies are small (about 4 KB), are sent to the server with every request, can have an expiry, and can be marked HttpOnly so JavaScript can't read them, which makes them better for session tokens.

points.point: localStorage persists until it is cleared, while sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes.
Cookies are sent to the server with every request.
Cookies are much smaller than web storage.
HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript, making them safer for tokens.

html.q: What do the async and defer attributes do on a script tag?
html.answer: Normally a script blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and runs. With async, the script downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it's ready, interrupting parsing, in no guaranteed order; good for independent scripts like analytics. With defer, it downloads in parallel and runs after the HTML is parsed, in document order; good for scripts that need the DOM.

points.point: Without async or defer a script blocks HTML parsing.
async scripts run as soon as they download, in no guaranteed order.
defer scripts run after the HTML is parsed, in document order.

html.q: Tell me about a website you built from scratch. How did you structure the HTML and make it accessible?
html.answer: A strong answer describes the site and audience, how you structured the markup semantically, specific accessibility work (labels, alt text, keyboard navigation, contrast), how you tested it (Lighthouse, a screen reader), and what you'd improve.

html.q: Describe a time you fixed an accessibility or SEO problem on a website.
html.answer: A strong answer explains how the issue was found (audit, user report, Lighthouse), what was wrong, the specific fix, and the measurable improvement such as a better audit score or search ranking.

css.answer: Every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin, from the inside out. By default (content-box) width and height apply only to the content, so padding and border add to the total size. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes padding and border, which makes layouts easier to reason about.

points.point: The box model consists of content, padding, border and margin.
With content-box, padding and border are added to the width.
border-box includes padding and border in the element's width.

css.q: What is the difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid?
css.answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional: it lays items out in a row or a column and is great for aligning and distributing items within a component, like a navbar. Grid is two-dimensional: it controls rows and columns at the same time, which suits overall page layouts. They work well together, for example a grid page layout with flex components inside.

points.point: Flexbox is one-dimensional, handling either a row or a column.
Grid is two-dimensional, handling rows and columns together.
Flexbox suits component alignment while Grid suits page layouts.

css.answer: When several rules target the same element, the most specific one wins. Inline styles beat IDs, IDs beat classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, and those beat element selectors. If specificity is equal, the rule that comes later wins. !important overrides normal rules and should be avoided because it makes styles hard to maintain.

points.point: Inline styles beat IDs, which beat classes, which beat element selectors.
When specificity is equal, the rule defined last wins.
!important overrides specificity and should be used sparingly.

css.q: What are the different values of the position property?
css.answer: static is the default normal flow. relative offsets an element from its normal position and creates a positioning context. absolute removes the element from the flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor. fixed positions it relative to the viewport, so it stays put while scrolling. sticky acts relative until a scroll threshold and then sticks like fixed.

points.point: absolute positions an element relative to its nearest positioned ancestor.
fixed positions an element relative to the viewport.
relative offsets an element from its normal position.
sticky switches from relative to fixed when scrolling past a threshold.

css.q: How do you build a responsive layout?
css.answer: Start mobile first and add media queries for larger breakpoints. Use flexible layouts with Flexbox and Grid, relative units like %, rem, vw and fr instead of fixed pixels, and make images flexible with max-width: 100%. Include the viewport meta tag, and use functions like clamp() for fluid typography. Test on real devices or emulators.

points.point: Media queries apply styles at different screen sizes.
Relative units like percentages, rem or fr are used instead of fixed pixels.
A mobile-first approach starts with small screens.
The viewport meta tag is required for responsive pages.

css.q: What causes layout reflow and how do you write performant CSS animations?
css.answer: Changing geometry, such as width, height, top or margin, forces the browser to recalculate layout (reflow) and repaint, which is expensive. Animating transform and opacity can be done on the compositor, often on the GPU, without layout or paint, so animations stay smooth. Avoid reading layout properties in between writes, which causes layout thrashing, and use will-change sparingly.

points.point: Changing properties like width, height or top triggers layout reflow.
Animating transform and opacity is cheap because it avoids layout and paint.
Interleaving layout reads and writes causes layout thrashing.

css.q: Tell me about a time you implemented a tricky UI design from a mockup.
css.answer: A strong answer explains the design and what made it tricky (responsive behaviour, complex layout, animation, browser support), the CSS approach you chose and why, problems you hit and how you solved them, and how you checked it across devices.

css.q: Describe a time you organised or refactored a large, messy stylesheet.
css.answer: A strong answer covers the problems (specificity wars, duplication, dead CSS), the approach (BEM, CSS modules, utility classes, design tokens), how you migrated safely (visual regression checks), and the outcome.

react.q: What is the virtual DOM and how does React use it?
react.answer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the UI. When state changes React renders a new virtual tree, compares it with the previous one (reconciliation, or diffing), and applies only the minimal set of changes to the real DOM, which is slower to update. Keys help React match list items between renders.

points.point: The virtual DOM is a JavaScript representation of the real DOM.
React compares the new virtual DOM with the previous one, which is called diffing or reconciliation.
React updates only the parts of the real DOM that changed.

react.q: What is the difference between state and props?
react.answer: Props are inputs passed from a parent to a child component and are read-only inside the child. State is data owned and managed by a component itself, changed with setState or a useState setter, and changing it triggers a re-render. Data flows down through props, and children notify parents through callback props.

points.point: Props are passed from a parent component and are read-only.
State is managed inside the component and can change.
Updating state triggers a re-render.

react.q: Explain the useEffect hook. What is the dependency array for?
react.answer: useEffect runs side effects, like fetching data, subscriptions or touching the DOM, after the component renders. The dependency array controls when it re-runs: with no array it runs after every render, with an empty array only after the first render, and otherwise whenever a listed value changes. Returning a function provides cleanup, which runs before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts.

points.point: useEffect runs side effects after the component renders.
An empty dependency array makes the effect run only once after the first render.
The effect re-runs when a value in the dependency array changes.
The returned cleanup function runs before re-running and on unmount.

react.q: Why do lists in React need keys, and why shouldn't you use the array index as a key?
react.answer: Keys let React identify which list items changed, were added or were removed, so it can reuse the right DOM nodes and component state during reconciliation. Keys must be stable and unique among siblings, like a database ID. Using the index breaks when items are inserted, removed or reordered: React matches the wrong items, causing state bugs and unnecessary re-renders.

points.point: Keys help React identify which items changed, were added or were removed.
Keys should be stable and unique, such as an ID.
Using the index as a key causes bugs when items are reordered, inserted or removed.

react.q: What are useMemo and useCallback, and when should you use them?
react.answer: useMemo caches the result of an expensive calculation between renders and recomputes it only when its dependencies change. useCallback caches a function definition so its identity stays the same, which matters when passing callbacks to children wrapped in React.memo or using them in effect dependencies. They add overhead, so use them for measured performance problems, not everywhere.

points.point: useMemo memoizes a computed value until its dependencies change.
useCallback memoizes a function so its reference stays the same between renders.
They are useful with React.memo children to prevent unnecessary re-renders.
They should only be used when there is a real performance problem.

react.q: How do you manage state in a large React application?
react.answer: Keep state as local as possible and lift it up only when components need to share it. Context avoids prop drilling for app-wide values like theme or the current user, but frequent updates through context re-render all consumers. For complex shared client state, use a store such as Redux Toolkit or Zustand, and for server data use a data-fetching library like React Query, which handles caching and refetching.

points.point: State should be kept local and lifted up only when it needs to be shared.
Context avoids prop drilling for global values.
Libraries like Redux or Zustand manage complex global state.
Server state is best handled with a library like React Query.

react.q: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?
react.answer: In a controlled component, form values live in React state: the input's value comes from state and onChange updates it, so React is the single source of truth and you can validate on every keystroke. In an uncontrolled component the DOM keeps the value and you read it with a ref when needed, which is simpler for basic forms or file inputs.

points.point: Controlled components store form values in React state.
Uncontrolled components keep the value in the DOM and read it with a ref.

react.q: What are custom hooks and why would you write one?
react.answer: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks. It extracts reusable stateful logic, like fetching data, form handling or subscribing to window size, so several components can share it without duplicating code. Each component that uses the hook gets its own independent state.

points.point: A custom hook is a function starting with use that calls other hooks.
Custom hooks let components reuse stateful logic.
Each component using a custom hook gets its own state.

react.q: How do you find and fix performance problems in a React app?
react.answer: First measure with the React DevTools Profiler to see which components re-render and why. Common fixes are avoiding unnecessary re-renders with React.memo, useMemo and useCallback, keeping state close to where it's used, virtualising long lists, code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense, and avoiding creating new objects in props on every render.

points.point: The React DevTools Profiler shows which components re-render.
React.memo prevents unnecessary re-renders of components.
Long lists can be virtualised so only visible items render.
Code splitting with React.lazy reduces the initial bundle size.

react.q: Tell me about a React application you built. How did you structure components and state?
react.answer: A strong answer explains the app and your role, how you split it into components, where state lived and why (local, context, a store, React Query), a concrete challenge, how you solved it, and the result.

react.q: Describe a time you fixed a performance problem or a re-rendering bug in React.
react.answer: A strong answer covers the symptom, how you measured it (Profiler, why-did-you-render), the root cause (unstable props, context updates, heavy computations, a missing effect dependency), the fix, and the measured improvement.

react.q: Tell me about a time you had to integrate a React frontend with a backend API. What problems did you face?
react.answer: A strong answer describes the API and data flow, how you handled loading, errors and caching, issues like CORS, authentication tokens or inconsistent data, how you coordinated with the backend, and the outcome.

angular.q: What are the main building blocks of an Angular application?
angular.answer: Components combine a TypeScript class with a template and styles and make up the UI. Services hold shared logic and data and are provided through dependency injection. Directives change DOM behaviour, pipes transform values in templates, and the router maps URLs to components. Older apps group these in NgModules; newer ones use standalone components.

points.point: Components combine a class with a template and make up the UI.
Services hold shared logic and are provided with dependency injection.
Directives and pipes extend templates.
Modules or standalone components organise the application.

angular.q: How does dependency injection work in Angular?
angular.answer: Classes declare what they need in their constructor (or with inject()), and Angular's injector creates and supplies those dependencies. Services are marked @Injectable and provided at a level such as providedIn: 'root', which gives one singleton for the app, or in a component's providers for a separate instance. This makes code modular and easy to test with mocks.

points.point: Dependencies are requested in the constructor and supplied by Angular's injector.
providedIn root creates a single shared instance of a service.
Dependency injection makes components easier to test.

angular.q: What are Observables in Angular and how are they different from Promises?
angular.answer: Angular uses RxJS Observables for HTTP, forms and events. A Promise produces a single value and starts immediately; an Observable can emit many values over time, is lazy until subscribed, and can be cancelled by unsubscribing. Operators like map, filter, switchMap and debounceTime transform streams. Unsubscribe, or use the async pipe, to avoid memory leaks.

points.point: Observables can emit multiple values over time while Promises resolve once.
Observables are lazy and only run when subscribed.
Observables can be cancelled by unsubscribing.
RxJS operators like map and switchMap transform observables.

angular.q: Explain Angular change detection and the OnPush strategy.
angular.answer: Angular checks component bindings and updates the DOM when something may have changed, triggered by events, HTTP responses and timers (traditionally via Zone.js). By default it checks the whole component tree. With ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush, a component is checked only when an input reference changes, an event fires inside it, an async pipe emits, or it's marked manually, which improves performance and pairs well with immutable data. Signals give even finer-grained updates.

points.point: Change detection checks bindings and updates the DOM after events, HTTP calls or timers.
The default strategy checks the whole component tree.
OnPush checks a component only when its input references change or an event occurs.
OnPush works well with immutable data and improves performance.

angular.q: What is the difference between template-driven and reactive forms?
angular.answer: Template-driven forms are defined mostly in the template with ngModel and suit simple forms. Reactive forms are defined in the component class with FormGroup and FormControl, are synchronous and explicit, easier to unit test, and better for dynamic forms and complex validation.

points.point: Template-driven forms are defined in the template using ngModel.
Reactive forms are defined in the component class with FormGroup and FormControl.
Reactive forms are better for complex validation and testing.

angular.q: Tell me about an Angular application you worked on and a difficult problem you solved in it.
angular.answer: A strong answer explains the app, your role, its structure (modules or standalone components, services, state), the specific problem (performance, RxJS complexity, forms, upgrades), how you solved it, and the outcome.

angular.q: Describe a time you upgraded an Angular version or migrated a legacy frontend.
angular.answer: A strong answer covers why the upgrade was needed, how you planned it (update guide, incremental steps, feature flags), breaking changes you hit, how you tested, and how long it took and what improved.

vue.q: How does reactivity work in Vue?
vue.answer: Vue wraps state in reactive proxies (ref and reactive in Vue 3). When a component renders it tracks which reactive values it reads, and when one of them changes Vue re-runs only the affected effects and re-renders the components that depend on it. Values accessed with ref need .value in script but are unwrapped in templates.

points.point: Vue tracks which reactive data a component uses during rendering.
Vue 3 uses JavaScript proxies for reactivity.
When reactive data changes, dependent components re-render automatically.
ref and reactive create reactive state.

vue.q: What is the difference between computed properties and watchers?
vue.answer: A computed property derives a value from reactive state and is cached until its dependencies change, so it's ideal for values shown in the template. A watcher runs a side effect when a value changes, like calling an API or saving to localStorage, and doesn't return a value.

points.point: Computed properties derive values and are cached until dependencies change.
Watchers run side effects when data changes.

vue.q: What is the Composition API and how does it differ from the Options API?
vue.answer: The Options API organises a component by option type: data, methods, computed and watch. The Composition API, used in setup or script setup, organises code by feature using functions like ref, computed and watch. That makes it easier to group related logic, extract reusable composables and get good TypeScript support.

points.point: The Options API organises code by option type such as data, methods and computed.
The Composition API organises code by feature inside setup.
The Composition API makes logic reusable through composables.
The Composition API has better TypeScript support.

vue.q: How do components communicate in Vue?
vue.answer: Parents pass data down with props, and children send messages up by emitting events that parents listen to. v-model is shorthand for a prop plus an update event. For deeply nested components you can use provide and inject, and for app-wide state a store like Pinia.

points.point: Parents pass data to children with props.
Children communicate with parents by emitting events.
provide/inject or a store like Pinia share state across many components.

vue.q: What is the difference between v-if and v-show?
vue.answer: v-if conditionally renders: the element is created or destroyed when the condition changes, so it has a higher toggle cost but nothing is rendered when false. v-show always renders the element and toggles CSS display, so the initial render costs more but toggling is cheap. Use v-show for things toggled often.

points.point: v-if adds or removes the element from the DOM.
v-show toggles the CSS display property.
v-show is better for frequent toggling.

vue.q: Tell me about a Vue application you built and how you managed its state.
vue.answer: A strong answer explains the app and your role, how components were organised, how state was managed (props and events, Pinia/Vuex, composables), a concrete challenge and how you solved it, and the result.

vue.q: Describe a time you migrated a Vue 2 app to Vue 3 or refactored to the Composition API.
vue.answer: A strong answer covers the motivation, the migration plan (compat build, incremental component conversion), breaking changes and library issues you hit, how you tested, and the outcome.

django.answer: Django follows Model-View-Template. Models define the data and map to database tables through the ORM. Views receive requests, apply business logic, query models and return responses. Templates render HTML with the data. URLconf routes each URL to a view, and Django itself plays the role of the controller.

points.point: Models define the data structure and map to database tables.
Views handle requests and contain the business logic.
Templates render the HTML shown to the user.
URL configuration routes URLs to views.

django.q: How does the Django ORM work, and what are select_related and prefetch_related?
django.answer: The ORM lets you query the database with Python using model managers and QuerySets, which are lazy and only hit the database when evaluated. Accessing related objects in a loop causes the N+1 problem. select_related follows foreign keys and one-to-one relations with a SQL join in a single query; prefetch_related runs a separate query for many-to-many or reverse relations and joins them in Python.

points.point: QuerySets are lazy and only query the database when evaluated.
select_related uses a SQL join for foreign key relationships.
prefetch_related runs a separate query for many-to-many relationships.
These methods prevent the N+1 query problem.

django.answer: Migrations are version-controlled files that describe changes to your models so the database schema can evolve. makemigrations generates them by comparing models with the previous state, and migrate applies them to the database. They should be committed to source control and reviewed, and data migrations can transform existing rows.

points.point: Migrations apply model changes to the database schema.
makemigrations creates migration files and migrate applies them.
Migration files are kept in version control.

django.answer: Middleware is a chain of hooks that processes every request before it reaches the view and every response on the way back. Django uses it for sessions, authentication, CSRF protection and security headers, and you can write your own for logging, timing or custom headers. The order in the MIDDLEWARE setting matters.

points.point: Middleware processes every request and response globally.
Django uses middleware for sessions, authentication and CSRF protection.
The order of middleware in settings matters.

django.q: How does Django protect against common web vulnerabilities?
django.answer: Templates auto-escape output to prevent XSS. The CSRF middleware requires a token on unsafe form submissions. The ORM uses parameterised queries, preventing SQL injection. It also offers clickjacking protection with X-Frame-Options, secure password hashing, and settings such as SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT and secure cookies. Running the deployment checklist (check --deploy) catches misconfiguration.

points.point: Templates auto-escape output to prevent cross-site scripting.
CSRF tokens protect forms against cross-site request forgery.
The ORM uses parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection.
Django hashes passwords securely.

django.q: Tell me about a Django project you built. How did you structure the apps and models?
django.answer: A strong answer explains the product and your role, how you split it into apps, key models and relationships, use of Django REST Framework or admin, a concrete challenge (performance, permissions, migrations), and the outcome.

django.q: Describe a time you optimised slow database queries in a Django application.
django.answer: A strong answer covers how you found the slow queries (Django Debug Toolbar, logging, APM), the cause (N+1, missing indexes, loading too much data), fixes like select_related, prefetch_related, only(), indexes or caching, and before-and-after numbers.

flask.q: What is Flask and how does it differ from Django?
flask.answer: Flask is a lightweight micro-framework: it provides routing, request handling and templating with Jinja2, and you add extensions for the database, auth, forms and so on. Django is batteries-included, with an ORM, admin, auth and migrations built in. Flask gives more flexibility and less structure, so it suits small services and APIs; Django suits larger apps that benefit from conventions.

points.point: Flask is a lightweight micro-framework.
Django is batteries-included with an ORM, admin and authentication built in.
Flask relies on extensions for features like databases and authentication.
Flask gives more flexibility while Django is more opinionated.

flask.answer: Blueprints group related routes, templates and static files into reusable components, like an auth blueprint or an API blueprint, often with a URL prefix. They are registered on the app with register_blueprint, which keeps large applications modular and works with the application factory pattern.

points.point: Blueprints organise related routes into modular components.
Blueprints are registered on the app with register_blueprint.
Blueprints can have a URL prefix.

flask.q: What is the application factory pattern in Flask?
flask.answer: Instead of creating the app at import time, you write a create_app function that builds the Flask app, loads configuration, initialises extensions with init_app and registers blueprints. This lets you create multiple apps with different configs, which is essential for testing, and avoids circular imports.

points.point: A create_app function builds and configures the Flask app.
The factory makes it easy to create apps with different configurations for testing.
Extensions are initialised with init_app inside the factory.
The factory pattern helps avoid circular imports.

flask.q: Explain the application and request contexts in Flask.
flask.answer: Flask uses context-local proxies so code can access request data without passing it around. The request context provides request and session for the current request. The application context provides current_app and g, which stores data for one request. Contexts are pushed automatically during a request; in scripts, background threads or tests you push one manually with app.app_context().

points.point: The request context provides the request and session objects.
The application context provides current_app and g.
Outside a request, such as in background jobs, you must push an app context manually.

flask.q: How do you handle database access in a Flask application?
flask.answer: Most Flask apps use Flask-SQLAlchemy: define models as classes, query them through the session, and commit or roll back transactions. Flask-Migrate (Alembic) handles schema migrations. Sessions are scoped to the request and cleaned up after it. Configure the database URL through config or environment variables rather than hard-coding it.

points.point: Flask-SQLAlchemy is commonly used as the ORM.
Flask-Migrate or Alembic manages schema migrations.
Changes are committed or rolled back in a database session.
The database URL should come from configuration or environment variables.

flask.q: How would you secure a Flask API?
flask.answer: Authenticate requests with sessions via Flask-Login or with tokens like JWT, and check authorisation on every endpoint. Validate and sanitise all input, use the ORM or parameterised queries, enable CSRF protection for forms, configure CORS narrowly, keep SECRET_KEY secret and never run with debug mode in production, use HTTPS, and rate-limit sensitive endpoints.

points.point: Requests are authenticated with sessions or tokens such as JWT.
All user input must be validated.
Debug mode must be disabled in production.
Use HTTPS and rate limiting.

flask.q: Tell me about a Flask application or API you built. How did you structure it?
flask.answer: A strong answer explains what the app did and your role, its structure (application factory, blueprints, services, database layer), how you handled config, auth and errors, a concrete challenge, and the outcome.

flask.q: Describe a time you deployed a Flask app to production. What issues did you run into?
flask.answer: A strong answer covers the deployment setup (Gunicorn or uWSGI, a reverse proxy, Docker, cloud platform), configuration and secrets, problems like timeouts, static files or database connections, how you debugged them, and what you monitored afterwards.

rest api.q: What are the main principles of a RESTful API?
rest api.answer: REST models everything as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods. It is stateless: each request contains all the information needed, and the server stores no client session. Responses use standard status codes and representations like JSON, can be cacheable, and the interface is uniform, with a client-server separation.

points.point: Resources are identified by URLs.
REST uses standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
REST APIs are stateless, so each request contains all needed information.
Responses use standard HTTP status codes.

rest api.q: What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST?
rest api.answer: POST creates a new resource, usually in a collection, and isn't idempotent: sending it twice creates two resources. PUT replaces a resource entirely at a known URL and is idempotent. PATCH partially updates a resource, sending only the changed fields.

points.point: POST creates a new resource.
PUT replaces the entire resource.
PATCH partially updates a resource.
PUT is idempotent while POST is not.

rest api.q: Explain the common HTTP status codes an API should return.
rest api.answer: 2xx means success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content. 4xx means the client made an error: 400 Bad Request for invalid input, 401 Unauthorized when not authenticated, 403 Forbidden when authenticated but not allowed, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict and 429 Too Many Requests. 5xx means a server error, like 500 Internal Server Error or 503 Service Unavailable.

points.point: 2xx status codes mean success, such as 200 OK and 201 Created.
4xx status codes mean client errors, such as 400 and 404.
401 means unauthenticated while 403 means forbidden.
5xx status codes mean server errors.

rest api.q: What does idempotency mean for an API and why does it matter?
rest api.answer: An operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. It matters because networks fail and clients retry: retrying an idempotent request is safe. For non-idempotent operations like payments, APIs accept an idempotency key so the server can detect and ignore duplicates.

points.point: An idempotent operation has the same effect no matter how many times it is repeated.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent while POST is not.
Idempotency makes retries safe after network failures.
Idempotency keys prevent duplicate processing of requests like payments.

rest api.q: How would you version a REST API?
rest api.answer: Common options are a version in the URL path (/api/v1/users), a custom header or Accept header media type, or a query parameter. URL versioning is the most visible and easiest to route and cache. Avoid breaking changes where possible by only adding fields, and when you must break, release a new version and deprecate the old one with a clear timeline.

points.point: The version can be placed in the URL path, such as /v1/.
The version can be sent in a header.
Old versions should be deprecated with a timeline.
Backward-compatible changes avoid the need for a new version.

rest api.q: How do you design pagination, filtering and sorting for an API that returns large lists?
rest api.answer: Never return unbounded lists. Offset/limit pagination is simple but slows down and can skip or repeat items on large or changing data; cursor-based pagination uses an opaque pointer to the last item and is stable and fast. Filtering and sorting use query parameters like ?status=active&sort=-created_at, backed by database indexes. Return the next cursor or links in the response.

points.point: Offset and limit pagination is simple but slow for large offsets.
Cursor-based pagination is more efficient and stable for large datasets.
Filtering and sorting are done with query parameters.
Database indexes support efficient filtering and sorting.

rest api.q: How do you secure a REST API?
rest api.answer: Use HTTPS everywhere. Authenticate with tokens such as OAuth 2.0 access tokens or JWTs, and check authorisation on every request, including that the user owns the resource. Validate all input, rate-limit to stop abuse, configure CORS narrowly, avoid leaking internal details in errors, and log and monitor access.

points.point: Use HTTPS to encrypt traffic.
Authenticate requests with tokens such as OAuth or JWT.
Check authorisation on every request, including resource ownership.
Validate input and apply rate limiting.

rest api.q: Tell me about an API you designed. What decisions did you make and why?
rest api.answer: A strong answer explains who consumed the API, how you modelled resources and endpoints, decisions on auth, errors, pagination and versioning, how you documented it (OpenAPI/Swagger), a trade-off you made, and how it worked out.

rest api.q: Describe a time an API you built or used had a breaking change or outage. How was it handled?
rest api.answer: A strong answer covers what broke and its impact, how it was detected, the immediate fix or rollback, communication with consumers, and the longer-term change (versioning, contract tests, monitoring).

graphql.q: What is GraphQL and how does it differ from REST?
graphql.answer: GraphQL is a query language for APIs where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs, usually through a single endpoint. REST exposes many endpoints with fixed response shapes, which can over-fetch or need several round trips. GraphQL has a strongly typed schema describing all data and operations, which enables tooling and introspection.

points.point: In GraphQL the client requests exactly the fields it needs.
GraphQL usually uses a single endpoint while REST uses many.
GraphQL avoids over-fetching and under-fetching.
GraphQL has a strongly typed schema.

graphql.q: What are queries, mutations and subscriptions in GraphQL?
graphql.answer: Queries read data. Mutations change data, such as creating or updating records, and return the result. Subscriptions keep a long-lived connection, usually over WebSockets, so the server can push updates to the client in real time when data changes.

points.point: Queries read or fetch data.
Mutations create, update or delete data.
Subscriptions push real-time updates, usually over WebSockets.

graphql.answer: A resolver is a function that returns the data for one field in the schema. The server executes a query by calling resolvers for each requested field, passing the parent object, arguments and context. Resolvers can fetch from databases, other services or REST APIs, which is why GraphQL works well as a layer over existing backends.

points.point: A resolver is a function that returns the data for a field.
Resolvers receive the parent object, arguments and context.
Resolvers can fetch data from databases or other services.

graphql.q: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how does DataLoader solve it?
graphql.answer: If a query asks for a list of posts with each post's author, a naive author resolver runs one database query per post, giving 1 + N queries. DataLoader batches all the keys requested during one tick into a single query (WHERE id IN ...) and caches results per request, collapsing N queries into one.

points.point: Nested resolvers can run one query per item, causing N+1 queries.
DataLoader batches multiple requests into a single query.
DataLoader caches results within a request.

graphql.q: How do you protect a GraphQL API from expensive or malicious queries?
graphql.answer: Because clients write their own queries, one deeply nested query can overload the server. Limit query depth and complexity or cost, set timeouts and rate limits, paginate list fields, and consider persisted queries so only approved queries run in production. Disable introspection in production if the schema shouldn't be public, and do authorisation in resolvers.

points.point: Limit query depth to prevent deeply nested queries.
Use query complexity or cost analysis.
Rate limiting and timeouts protect the server.
Persisted queries allow only approved queries.

graphql.q: Tell me about a project where you used GraphQL. Why did you choose it over REST?
graphql.answer: A strong answer explains the project and clients, the specific reasons GraphQL fit (multiple clients with different needs, nested data, reducing round trips), how you designed the schema, a challenge like N+1 or caching, and whether it paid off.

graphql.q: Describe a time you debugged a slow GraphQL query.
graphql.answer: A strong answer covers how the slowness was noticed, the tools used (tracing, resolver timing, query logs), the root cause (N+1, over-fetching from the database, a slow downstream service), the fix (DataLoader, caching, schema change), and the improvement.

json.q: What is JSON and what data types does it support?
json.answer: JSON, JavaScript Object Notation, is a lightweight text format for exchanging data that's easy for people to read and machines to parse. It supports objects (key-value pairs with string keys), arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. It has no date type or comments, so dates are usually sent as ISO 8601 strings.

points.point: JSON is a lightweight text format for data exchange.
JSON supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
JSON has no date type, so dates are sent as strings.

json.q: What is the difference between JSON and XML?
json.answer: JSON is more compact and maps directly to data structures in most languages, so it's faster to parse and easier to work with; it's the default for web APIs. XML is more verbose, uses tags with attributes, supports namespaces, comments and mixed content, and has mature schema and validation tooling, so it's still common in enterprise and document formats.

points.point: JSON is more compact and less verbose than XML.
JSON maps naturally to data structures and is easier to parse.
XML supports attributes, namespaces and comments.

json.q: What is JSON Schema and why use it?
json.answer: JSON Schema is a JSON document that describes the expected structure of other JSON: required fields, types, formats, ranges and allowed values. You use it to validate API requests and responses, configuration files and messages, generate documentation, and catch bad data early. OpenAPI uses a JSON Schema dialect to describe API payloads.

points.point: JSON Schema describes the expected structure and types of JSON data.
JSON Schema is used to validate data.
OpenAPI uses JSON Schema to describe API payloads.

json.q: What are the security risks of parsing JSON and how do you mitigate them?
json.answer: Never parse JSON with eval, which runs arbitrary code; use a real parser like JSON.parse or json.loads. Validate the parsed data against an expected schema instead of trusting it, limit payload size and nesting depth to avoid denial of service, be careful with deserialisation libraries that instantiate arbitrary types, and watch for prototype pollution in JavaScript when merging parsed objects.

points.point: JSON should never be parsed with eval.
Parsed data should be validated against an expected schema.
Limit payload size and nesting depth to prevent denial of service.
Unsafe deserialisation or prototype pollution can lead to attacks.

json.q: Tell me about a time you designed a JSON data format or API payload. What did you consider?
json.answer: A strong answer explains the use case and consumers, decisions on naming, nesting, nulls, dates and IDs, how you documented and validated it, how you planned for future changes, and the result.

json.q: Describe a time bad or unexpected JSON data caused a bug. How did you fix it?
json.answer: A strong answer covers the symptom, how you traced it to the data (logs, payload inspection), the root cause (missing field, wrong type, encoding, timezone), the fix, and the safeguard you added such as schema validation or defensive parsing.

authentication.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
authentication.answer: Authentication verifies who a user is, for example with a password, a one-time code or a token. Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do, such as which resources they can read or change, often with roles or permissions. Authentication happens first; authorization is checked on every protected action.

points.point: Authentication verifies a user's identity.
Authorization determines what a user is allowed to do.
Authorization is often implemented with roles or permissions.

authentication.answer: Never store plain-text or reversibly encrypted passwords. Store a hash created with a slow, salted password-hashing algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. The unique salt per password defeats rainbow tables, and the deliberate slowness (work factor) makes brute-forcing leaked hashes expensive. Fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone are not suitable.

points.point: Passwords must be hashed, never stored in plain text.
Each password hash uses a unique salt.
Slow algorithms like bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 should be used.
Fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 are not suitable for passwords.

authentication.q: Compare session-based authentication with token-based authentication using JWTs.
authentication.answer: With sessions, the server stores session state and the browser holds a session ID in a cookie; logging out or revoking access is easy, but the server needs shared session storage to scale. With JWTs, the token itself contains signed claims, so servers can verify it without a lookup, which suits APIs and microservices, but tokens are hard to revoke before expiry, so they should be short-lived and paired with refresh tokens.

points.point: Session-based authentication stores session state on the server.
A JWT contains signed claims and is stateless.
Sessions are easy to revoke while JWTs are hard to revoke before expiry.
JWTs should be short-lived and used with refresh tokens.

authentication.q: What is multi-factor authentication and how does TOTP work?
authentication.answer: MFA requires two or more different factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone or security key) and something you are (biometrics). TOTP apps share a secret with the server when you enrol; both compute a code from the secret and the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so the codes match without any network call. Hardware keys using WebAuthn are even stronger because they resist phishing.

points.point: MFA combines factors like something you know, have and are.
TOTP generates codes from a shared secret and the current time.
Hardware keys with WebAuthn resist phishing.

authentication.q: How do you protect a login system against attacks?
authentication.answer: Rate-limit and lock out or slow down repeated failed attempts to stop brute force and credential stuffing, and offer MFA. Use generic error messages so attackers can't enumerate accounts. Protect forms with CSRF tokens, set session cookies as HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, regenerate the session ID after login to prevent fixation, use HTTPS, and check passwords against breached-password lists.

points.point: Rate limiting and lockouts prevent brute force attacks.
Generic error messages prevent account enumeration.
Cookies should be HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
The session ID should be regenerated after login.
MFA protects against stolen passwords.

authentication.q: Tell me about an authentication or login system you implemented.
authentication.answer: A strong answer explains the requirements, the approach (sessions, JWT, OAuth/SSO, an identity provider), how you stored credentials and handled password reset, security measures you added, a challenge you hit, and the outcome.

authentication.q: Describe a time you found or fixed a security issue related to authentication or access control.
authentication.answer: A strong answer covers how the issue was discovered, what the flaw was (missing authorization check, token leakage, weak reset flow), its potential impact, the fix, and the process change that prevented similar issues.

oauth.q: What is OAuth 2.0 and what problem does it solve?
oauth.answer: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that lets an application access a user's resources on another service without getting the user's password. The user approves limited access (scopes) on the provider's site, and the app receives an access token to call the API. It's about delegated authorization, not authentication on its own.

points.point: OAuth lets an app access a user's resources without the user's password.
OAuth is an authorization framework for delegated access.
The app receives an access token limited by scopes.

oauth.q: Explain the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE.
oauth.answer: The app redirects the user to the authorization server with a code challenge derived from a random code verifier. The user logs in and consents, and is redirected back with a short-lived authorization code. The app exchanges the code plus the original code verifier at the token endpoint for an access token (and often a refresh token). PKCE ensures a stolen authorization code can't be redeemed by an attacker, so it's recommended for all clients, especially mobile and single-page apps.

points.point: The user is redirected to the authorization server to log in and consent.
The app receives an authorization code and exchanges it for an access token.
PKCE uses a code verifier and code challenge.
PKCE prevents a stolen authorization code from being used.

oauth.q: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
oauth.answer: OAuth 2.0 handles authorization: it gives an app an access token to call APIs. OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that handles authentication: it adds an ID token, a JWT with information about who the user is, plus a userinfo endpoint and standard scopes like openid, profile and email. 'Sign in with Google' uses OpenID Connect.

points.point: OAuth 2.0 is for authorization while OpenID Connect is for authentication.
OpenID Connect is built on top of OAuth 2.0.
OpenID Connect adds an ID token, which is a JWT describing the user.

oauth.q: What is the difference between access tokens and refresh tokens?
oauth.answer: An access token is sent with API requests to prove permission and is short-lived, often minutes to an hour, to limit damage if it leaks. A refresh token is long-lived, sent only to the authorization server, and used to get new access tokens without the user logging in again. Refresh tokens must be stored securely and can be rotated and revoked.

points.point: Access tokens are short-lived and used to call APIs.
Refresh tokens are used to obtain new access tokens without logging in again.
Refresh tokens are long-lived and must be stored securely.

oauth.answer: Scopes define what an access token is allowed to do, such as read:email or calendar.write. The app requests scopes, the user sees and approves them on the consent screen, and the resource server checks the token's scopes before allowing an action. Apps should request the minimum scopes they need.

points.point: Scopes limit what an access token is allowed to do.
The user approves the requested scopes on a consent screen.
Apps should request the minimum scopes they need.

oauth.q: Tell me about a time you integrated 'Sign in with Google' or another OAuth provider.
oauth.answer: A strong answer explains why you used it, the flow you implemented (authorization code with PKCE, a library), how you handled tokens, user accounts and linking, problems like redirect URIs or token expiry, and the result.

oauth.q: Describe a time you secured an API that third parties or other services accessed.
oauth.answer: A strong answer covers who the clients were, the auth mechanism chosen (client credentials, API keys, OAuth scopes, mTLS), how you managed and rotated credentials, monitoring and rate limits, and any incident or lesson learned.
